# Kubernetes Teams Trust Automation to Ship Code—But Not to Touch CPU

Most Kubernetes teams automated deployments years ago. They'll let a pipeline push code to production dozens of times a day without a second thought. But ask that same team to let automation adjust CPU requests? Suddenly everyone wants a human in the loop.

That gap—between what we trust automation to do and what we don't—is about to get a lot more interesting as AI tooling moves deeper into resource management.

## What's Actually Happening

Kubernetes teams have gotten comfortable with a specific kind of automation. CI/CD pipelines run constantly. Autoscaling adjusts replica counts based on load. GitOps workflows reconcile cluster state against declared configs. This is table stakes now.

But there's a clear boundary most teams don't cross: letting automation touch the actual resource definitions. CPU requests. Memory limits. The numbers that determine whether your workload gets scheduled, whether it gets throttled, or whether it gets evicted when things get tight.

The pattern I'm seeing is consistent. Teams will automate everything around resource management—deployment, scaling, monitoring—but draw a hard line at having automation change the resource specs themselves. Those still get set manually, reviewed in PRs, and updated reluctantly.

Why the disconnect? Deployments are recoverable. You push bad code, you roll back. Takes minutes. But resource misconfigurations compound differently. Set CPU requests too low, and you get throttling that degrades performance in ways that are hard to trace. Set them too high, and you're wasting capacity across every replica—costs that accumulate silently until someone audits the bill.

The blast radius feels different, even if objectively the risk of a bad deployment might be higher.

## The AI Variable

Here's where it gets more complicated. AI-powered tools are starting to offer automated resource optimization for Kubernetes workloads. The pitch is straightforward: let the system observe actual usage patterns, recommend adjustments, and—if you trust it enough—apply those adjustments automatically.

These tools range from recommendation-only (you still click the button) to fully autonomous (the system adjusts resources on its own schedule). The value proposition is real. Most teams overprovision because it's the safe default. Rightsizing could cut costs significantly. And doing it manually at scale is tedious enough that it rarely happens.

But here's the tension: the same teams that hesitate to let simple threshold-based automation touch CPU requests are now being asked to hand that authority to AI systems they understand even less.

It's not an irrational hesitation. Traditional automation follows rules you wrote. You can trace the logic. When an autoscaler adds replicas, you know exactly why—the metric crossed the threshold you defined. But when an AI system decides your service needs 200m CPU instead of 500m, the reasoning is opaque. It learned from patterns. Which patterns? Good luck auditing that.

## Why Practitioners Should Care

This isn't just a philosophical question about automation philosophy. It has concrete implications for how teams operate.

**Cost pressure is increasing.** Cloud bills matter more than they did two years ago. Finance teams are asking harder questions. The inefficiency of manual resource management—or the "set it high and forget it" approach—is becoming less acceptable. Teams that don't find a way to rightsize are going to face pressure from above.

**Toil is real.** For teams that do try to manage resources manually, the work never ends. Usage patterns change. Traffic shifts. New features alter resource profiles. Keeping specs accurate across dozens or hundreds of services is a losing battle. Most teams just don't do it, which means they're either overpaying or underprovisioned without knowing it.

**Incident complexity increases.** When resource-related issues do occur—throttling, OOM kills, scheduling failures—troubleshooting is painful. If a human set those numbers months ago based on gut feel, good luck reconstructing the rationale. If an AI system set them, you're adding another layer of "why did this happen" to the investigation.

**The trust question affects adoption speed.** Teams that figure out how to trust AI-driven resource management—with appropriate guardrails—will move faster. Teams that don't will either burn engineering time on manual optimization or accept the inefficiency tax. Neither is great.

### The Guardrail Problem

The obvious answer is "use AI recommendations but keep humans in the loop." And that works, to a point. But it creates its own problems.

If every AI recommendation requires manual review and approval, you've just created a new approval queue. Engineers start rubber-stamping because they don't have time to deeply evaluate every suggestion. Or recommendations pile up and never get applied because no one owns the task.

The middle ground—applying changes automatically within defined bounds—requires defining those bounds well. What's the maximum percentage change allowed? How frequently can adjustments happen? What workloads are excluded entirely? These aren't trivial questions, and most teams haven't thought through them.

The tooling maturity varies too. Some solutions offer dry-run modes, gradual rollouts, automatic rollback if performance degrades. Others are more "trust us, we've got this." The difference matters a lot when you're deciding how much autonomy to grant.

## The Security Angle

There's another dimension here that doesn't get enough attention: resource definitions are a security boundary.

CPU and memory limits aren't just about cost optimization. They're a containment mechanism. A runaway process—whether from a bug or a compromise—gets bounded by those limits. If automation can adjust those limits upward without review, it's potentially weakening that containment.

This isn't theoretical. Cryptomining attacks against Kubernetes clusters have been documented. An attacker who can influence resource limits—even indirectly—has expanded their operational space.

I'm not saying AI-driven resource management is a security risk by default. But teams evaluating these tools should ask: Who can influence what the AI learns from? What prevents the system from gradually relaxing limits across the fleet? Are there hard caps that can't be overridden by automation?

Most teams aren't asking these questions yet because they're still thinking about this as purely a cost and performance problem.

## What to Watch

A few things will determine how this plays out over the next 12-18 months.

**Observability integration.** The AI systems that gain trust will be the ones that show their work. Not just "we recommend 200m CPU" but "here's the usage data, here's our confidence interval, here's what happens if we're wrong." Teams need to audit these decisions, especially after incidents.

**Rollback automation.** Changing a resource spec is easy. Knowing it caused a problem and reverting quickly is harder. Tools that can detect performance regression and automatically revert will earn more trust than tools that just make changes and walk away.

**Workload classification.** Not all workloads should get the same treatment. Your payment processing service probably shouldn't be subject to aggressive autonomous optimization. Your internal dev tooling might be fine. The platforms that let teams define these tiers—and enforce them—will be more adoptable.

**Incident postmortem tooling.** When something goes wrong, teams need to answer "what changed and why." If AI-driven resource changes are happening, they need to show up clearly in your audit trail. This sounds obvious but isn't always the case.

## What to Do Next

If you're evaluating AI-driven resource optimization—or just trying to improve your manual process—here's a practical starting point.

**Audit your current state.** Do you actually know how your resource requests compare to actual usage? Most teams don't. Before you can evaluate whether automation would help, you need to understand the gap you're working with. [UNVERIFIED: Some reports suggest the average Kubernetes workload requests 3-5x more CPU than it uses, but I haven't verified this independently.]

**Define your risk tiers.** Which workloads are you comfortable experimenting with? Which ones require human approval for any resource change? Make this explicit before you're configuring a new tool's policies.

**Start with recommendations, but set a timeline.** Recommendation-only mode is fine for learning. But if you're still manually approving every change six months later, you haven't actually solved the toil problem. Decide in advance: what would need to be true for us to trust automated application?

**Integrate with your incident process.** However you manage resource specs—manually, semi-automated, or fully autonomous—make sure changes are visible in your incident investigation workflow. Correlating a performance degradation with a resource change should take seconds, not hours.

**Ask the security questions early.** Before you deploy an optimizer, understand its threat model. What happens if it's fed bad data? What are the maximum changes it can make? Can it be constrained by hard policy limits that can't be overridden?

## The Bigger Picture

The Kubernetes automation trust gap isn't really about Kubernetes. It's about where we draw lines between "automation we understand" and "automation we're taking on faith."

CI/CD pipelines felt risky once. Now they're invisible infrastructure. Autoscaling was controversial; now it's expected. The question isn't whether resource optimization will eventually become automated—it's how we get there without the inevitable incidents that come from trusting systems we don't fully understand.

AI tooling is accelerating this timeline. The efficiency gains are real enough that teams will adopt these tools. The question is whether they'll adopt them thoughtfully, with appropriate guardrails, or reactively, after a cost crisis or outage forces the issue.

The teams that figure out how to extend trust incrementally—proving out automation in controlled contexts before expanding scope—will navigate this better than the teams that either refuse all automation or embrace it uncritically.

---

**The open question:** Where does your team draw the line on Kubernetes automation today—and has that line moved in the last year? I'm curious whether the pressure to adopt AI tooling is changing how teams think about what they're willing to let machines control.
